power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Reading is a fundamental life skill, and at its basis is the ability to process single words.
Researchers often study single-word processing using lexical decision tasks.
However, most research is conducted in a single language by separate research groups, limiting comparability, replicability, and generalizability.
In addition, best-practice knowledge is often only transmitted informally within labs, leading to heterogeneity and reduced reproducibility across labs.
Here, we, the TRUST Consortium, established a consensus-based research guideline for current best practices in psycholinguistic reading research by integrating expert knowledge.
We used German as a case study and formulated guidelines for visual lexical decision experiments.
We reached consortium-level consensus through multiple feedback circles and quantified agreement using importance ratings.

The guidelines are openly available as a living guideline document on a webpage (https://trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io/en/latest/), with git-versioning infrastructure that makes changes transparent and enables discussion.
text.formatted: The guidelines are openly available as a living guideline document on a webpage (<ref type="url" target="https://trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io</ref>), with git-versioning infrastructure that makes changes transparent and enables discussion.

text.text: To validate the guidelines, we implemented the German Lexicon Project, providing an empirical feedback loop to test our suggestions.
The living, open nature of the guidelines invites broader community feedback.

It also enables future extension to other languages, groups (e.g., dyslexics), and methods (e.g., brain imaging), as it is openly available and includes instructions for hosting an adapted version at no cost.

Thus, we provide a document intended to raise research standards in reading research worldwide, as a service to the community, potentially increasing replication rates and generalizability of relevant effects and phenomena.

text.text: Making rigorous research standards explicit and accessible can help researchers produce and evaluate such evidence [e.g., 14] and, consequently, increase trust in scientific discovery.
Within cognitive psychology, applying these standards requires attention to research questions, study designs, and participant characteristics.

Particularly, in language-related research, such as the study of reading, understanding how cognitive processing varies with language characteristics is central to understanding the phenomenon as a whole [6].

text.text: Efforts to articulate research standards in this area should therefore make their scope explicit and allow for contributions from researchers working across languages, populations, and methods.

Here, we provide a description of the TRansparent, sUStainable, and Transferable (TRUST) Guidelines for psycholinguistic reading studies: an open, living document with the goal of describing the research standards for psycholinguistic reading, based on the explicitly collected agreement of a group of reading research experts.
We wrote the guidelines with a target audience in mind that includes new researchers.
Open guidelines facilitate knowledge sharing with new researchers beyond individual labs, and we believe this also represents an important step toward increasing academic diversity in the field.
As a general goal, we aim to promote the development of consensus-based guidelines that span perspectives.

Our proposed guidelines can be easily expanded across domains: from basic to applied research, across languages, groups (e.g., multilinguals), and methodological approaches, for researchers with cognitive, educational, genetic, and neuroscientific foci.

Reading research has gained a wealth of insights from lexical decision paradigms (see Fig. 1), in which participants categorize lexical items (alphabetic strings of letters) as words or nonwords (e.g., [16, 8, 17]).

text.text: Progress has been made as materials, experiments, data, and analysis scripts have become more openly available.
Despite this, clear guidance or consensus on how best to implement and report a word-recognition study using lexical decision tasks remains lacking.

Such methodological heterogeneity compounds other sources of heterogeneity inherent in psycholinguistic research (e.g., differences between languages or individuals), impeding comparisons and the integration of findings across studies, especially when investigating disputed phenomena [e.g., 23].
Thus, when conflicting results are reported, it becomes difficult to integrate the findings into a coherent understanding of the processes underlying word recognition.

Rather than revealing theoretically relevant insights of TRUST 6 interest, differences between studies may instead stem from methodological choices, material-specific factors (e.g., effects differing between languages or stimulus sets), or participant-specific issues (e.g., effects differing between samples of a population), which can also inherently limit the informativeness of meta-analyses or systematic reviews, not to say that heterogeneity, when documented accurately, can be highly valuable.
To further complicate cross-lab comparisons, information on how to implement a task is often only transmitted informally within the lab [33].
text.formatted: To further complicate cross-lab comparisons, information on how to implement a task is often only transmitted informally within the lab <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Researchers often learn to conduct a study in a particular way (e.g., implementing a lexical decision task with a specific font or inter-stimulus interval) from established laboratory practices or methods reported in the literature.
These procedures may have been informed by theoretical considerations, previous evidence, or practical piloting, but the rationale for individual choices is not always explicitly documented.
Consequently, researchers adopting them may have limited information about why they were selected or whether they are appropriate for a new study.
Sometimes, such procedures are based on informal piloting and testing to reduce noise and maximize effect sizes.
Other choices lack justification and merely reflect the adoption of existing routines.
Often, there is no consensus on which specific methodological choices matter in a lexical decision task.
For example, we now know that how pseudoword foils are created affects word processing [16, 34, 35], a previously neglected issue because hypotheses largely focused on word reading.

text.text: As a starting point, we focused on typical readers reading in German.
We chose German as a starting point mainly because it is the primary language of expertise of the consortium.

text.text: By providing both the resulting guidelines and information on how to apply the consensus-building process, we aim to offer well-founded best-practice guidance to reading researchers of all experience levels.

The guidelines are intended for researchers designing, conducting, or reporting lexical decision studies of visual word recognition, including those new to the area and experienced researchers seeking methodological guidance.

The target audience includes cognitive and neurocognitive scientists unfamiliar with word recognition research, aspiring psycholinguistics researchers, and experienced researchers working across different domains of reading research.

Furthermore, the guidelines can help researchers justify specific methodological choices, supported by explicit agreement, or transparently report and justify any deviations from our proposed guidelines.

Researchers unfamiliar with German, or with the specifics of the German language, may also benefit from the guidelines, as they provide references to useful resources that introduce information specific to German language and orthography.

This could help researchers conducting cross-linguistic research [e.g., 23], those interested in theoretically relevant research questions that can be addressed by leveraging specific features of the German language [e.g., inflection; 46], or researchers relocating to a German-focused lab.
In doing so, we offer guidance to researchers with psycholinguistic expertise in other languages in transferring their research into German, even without personal proficiency in the language 1 .
To ensure the practicality and completeness of the guidelines, we developed them in parallel to an implementation of the German Lexicon Project, a megastudy of lexical decisions in German.

In the German Lexicon Project, TRUST Consortium members and additional associates tested the applicability of the guidelines by implementing them and collecting lexical decision data for tens of thousands of words and nonwords from thousands of participants across German-speaking countries.
We established the guidelines adhering to Open Science principles.
We implemented the guidelines as a living document, open to extensions and updates, with a platform supporting expert discussion as the guidelines evolve.

The main aims of the TRUST guidelines are: • Make methodological knowledge more accessible • Support transparent and reproducible research 1 Although theoretically, a lexical decision study can be conducted without knowledge of a language, it is advisable to consult speakers of the language to check the items when selecting and evaluating stimuli.

Such consultation can help identify unintended lexical, semantic, or cultural associations that may not be apparent from corpus-based measures and assess their relevance to the study (e.g., to remove words or pseudowords which may have negative cultural associations that are not evident from corpus data; examples in German may include terms that have an offensive connotation when used as slang).

Such that the guidelines provide best-practice guidance on procedures, materials, analysis, and reporting, promoting comparability across studies that use lexical decision tasks with adult readers in German.

By creating them, we aim to improve the accessibility of methodological knowledge in reading research and to propose a workflow that encourages and enables researchers to share their materials, procedures, analysis scripts, and data with the wider research community.

The guideline document is openly available and provides researchers across the behavioral and social sciences with a template for developing best-practice guidelines in their own tasks, fields, populations, or languages of interest.

text.text: The consortium was prompted by several key challenges identified and defined in the proposal relevant to reading research.
• Lack of methodological comparability and transparency across studies.
• Low variability of languages and orthographies studied.
• Small, homogeneous sample sizes.
• Low exploitation of computationally implemented hypotheses (i.e., computational models).
• Reproducibility issues and questionable research practices.
• Lack of fairness.
This prompted a discussion with the core group 3 on how to proceed.
We divided into four groups (Materials, Procedure, Analysis, and Reporting).
Within these groups, consortium members drafted and discussed an initial version of the guidelines, first within groups and then across groups during a three-day workshop in Cologne.

Furthermore, the consortium reached a general consensus that, in case of inconsistencies or when ad hoc decisions were needed during the process, the core group could resolve procedural inconsistencies and make ad hoc decisions when needed to avoid delays in developing the guidelines.

During this workshop, the consortium also agreed that an extensive German Lexicon Project with adult readers was needed and that such a project would be ideal for testing the applicability of the guidelines.
After the workshop, XS and BG consolidated the first draft of the guidelines.

text.text: This section comprises eleven subsections (∼1,940 words) addressing considerations for implementing a lexical decision experiment.

For example, there are subsections outlining considerations for programming the experiment (e.g., platforms, text encoding, trial structure), referencing resources for determining sample size via power analysis, and outlining possible participant inclusion criteria.
We describe different design options, including controlled experiments, semi-controlled regression designs (e.g., lexicon projects), and crowd-sourced projects.
The materials section includes 23 subsections (∼ 3,180 words) and addresses stimulus selection in general, as well as resources available for German more specifically.
One subsection describes where to find words most effectively (i.e., in available psycholinguistic corpora).
The next subsection describes variables to consider when characterizing words using psycholinguistic properties (e.g., word frequency).
We also discuss how to account for "taboo" words and German-specific issues related to inflections, compound words, parts of speech, lemmatization, and TRUST 13 word-characteristic-based filtering.
The guidelines similarly list variables to consider in nonword selection and recommend how best to create nonwords.
Analysis.

The analysis section of the guidelines provides recommendations for data preprocessing, transformation, and statistical analysis of lexical decision data from typical readers, in six subsections (∼ 1,960 words).

We describe sanity-check analyses (e.g., estimate the word frequency effect), discuss how best to assess the effect of interest (e.g., using crossed random effects with linear mixed models), and give some ideas about additional analysis options (e.g., model-based analysis).
Reporting.
The final reporting section of the guidelines addresses how to report the results of psycholinguistic studies of German in twelve subsections (∼ 1,350 words).
This section provides crucial information on how to maximize reproducibility while avoiding information irrelevant to the methodology or cognition of reading.

Here, we recommend how to report the rationale of a study, document procedures, contributions, and resources, and provide specific guidance on documenting methodology, experimental procedures, results, and analysis.
Finally, we recommend optimal data storage and sharing.

text.text: We describe best-practice consensus-based guidelines for implementing a lexical decision task for typical adult readers with a focus on German.
We obtained the guidelines through a consensus-finding procedure within the TRUST Consortium, which consists of expert reading researchers.
We identified and collated well-established practices across labs described in the procedure, materials, analysis, and reporting sections.
To validate the guidelines, we also implemented the German Lexicon Project All experts contributed content to the guidelines and gave feedback at multiple stages.

Our guidelines may be used as a template for implementing guideline documents for the same task in a different language, a different task in German, or for a consensus-building process in practice (see also [9] for an example in a different field).

text.text: In addition, the guidelines in their current form may not be fully complete, as the consortium may not encompass all relevant expertise, and some topics may have been overlooked or inadequately addressed.
However, the current guidelines, as a living document using GitHub, allow researchers beyond the consortium to comment on individual recommendations and propose additions or revisions.
From now on, researchers can change the TRUST guidelines using the established mechanism (e.g., raising an issue for discussion) already provided in the open repository.
As part of the guidelines creation process, consortium members provided importance ratings.
These importance ratings are provided alongside the title of each corresponding subsection in the guidelines document.
All items received median ratings of 4 or 5, showing that experts consistently identified the issues we focused on as important.
We also used the ratings to estimate consensus among members.
The results indicated relatively high consensus, as only a small fraction of items showed considerable differences between raters.

Inspecting the ratings for each part separately, we found that the analysis section, in particular, was the least controversial among experts, although all other sections showed similarly low divergence between raters.
Thus, we have evidence that the procedure effectively aggregated the knowledge of a medium-sized group of experts and produced a document with high consensus.
This result is not challenge: First, researchers must keep in mind that the information may not always reflect the most current best practice, as standards may have recently changed.
Second, a dedicated and enthusiastic community will play an important role in continuously monitoring and updating the guideline document.
Our open, consensus-based guideline document is a step towards increasing continuity in studies conducted across labs in reading research, concerned with visual word recognition.

We not only established and documented consensus about the guidelines, but also ensured they could serve as a template for similar initiatives seeking to reduce researchers' degrees of freedom across different languages, populations, and measurement tasks.
Furthermore, the guidelines are informed by their implementation in the German Lexicon Project, which successfully tested their applicability.

Thus, it offers not only a platform for methodological discussion but also the foundation for new, higher-quality studies to better understand human reading and word recognition processes across labs.
